tasks.title: A Poker Hand
tasks.context: A standard 52-card deck (13 ranks × 4 suits) is shuffled, and 5 cards are dealt at random to form a hand.
statements: The total number of distinct 5-card hands is 2,598,960.
A full house (three of one rank plus two of another) is more likely than four of a kind.
A flush (all five cards the same suit) is more likely than a full house.
The probability of getting two pair is greater than 5%.
The probability of a flush is more than 8 times the probability of four of a kind.
tactical_explanations:

$\binom{52}{5}$ = 2,598,960 exactly, as computed above.

$$
Total 5-card hands = \binom{52}{5}
$$

**Takeaway:** $\binom{52}{5}$ = 2,598,960 exactly, as computed above.

**Statement B — True**

Full house has 3,744 hands versus 624 for four of a kind, so a full house is indeed more likely — six times as likely, in

$$
Compare 13·\binom{4}{3}·12·\binom{4}{2} = 3,744 to 13·48 = 624
$$

**Takeaway:** Full house has 3,744 hands versus 624 for four of a kind, so a full house is indeed more likely — six times as likely, in
fact.

**Statement C — True**

A flush has 5,148 hands versus 3,744 for a full house, so a flush is more likely, even though both are rare.

$$
Compare \binom{13}{5}·4 = 5,148 to 13·\binom{4}{3}·12·\binom{4}{2} = 3,744
$$

**Takeaway:** A flush has 5,148 hands versus 3,744 for a full house, so a flush is more likely, even though both are rare.

P(two pair) = 123,552/2,598,960 ≈ 4.754%, which is not greater than 5% — a close call.

**Takeaway:** P(two pair) = 123,552/2,598,960 ≈ 4.754%, which is not greater than 5% — a close call.

The ratio of flush hands to four-of-a-kind hands is 5,148/624 = 8.25, which is indeed more than 8.

$$

**Takeaway:** The ratio of flush hands to four-of-a-kind hands is 5,148/624 = 8.25, which is indeed more than 8.

tasks.title: Rolling the Dice
tasks.context: 5 fair six-sided dice are rolled at once, and the 5 results are recorded in order (each die is distinguishable).
statements: The total number of possible outcomes is 7,776.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers is greater than 20%.
The probability that at least two dice show the same number is less than 80%.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers equals exactly 1/6.
If only 3 dice were rolled instead of 5, the probability of all different values would be lower than with 5 dice.
tactical_explanations:
**Statement A — True**

Each of the 5 dice has 6 possible outcomes, independently, giving 6⁵ = 7,776 total outcomes.

$$
Total outcomes = 6⁵
$$

**Takeaway:** Each of the 5 dice has 6 possible outcomes, independently, giving 6⁵ = 7,776 total outcomes.

**Statement B — False**

P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 9.26%, which is not greater than 20% — it is well below it.

$$
P(all different) = 6·5·4·3·2 / 6⁵
$$

**Close call:** P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 9.26%, which is not greater than 20% — it is well below it.

**Takeaway:** P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 9.26%, which is not greater than 20% — it is well below it.

**Statement C — False**

P(at least two the same) = 1 − 5/54 ≈ 90.74%, which is not less than 80% — it is considerably higher, since having any
repeat among 5 dice sharing only 6 faces is quite common (this is the same logic behind the birthday paradox).

$$
P(at least two same) = 1 − P(all different)
$$

**Takeaway:** P(at least two the same) = 1 − 5/54 ≈ 90.74%, which is not less than 80% — it is considerably higher, since having any
repeat among 5 dice sharing only 6 faces is quite common (this is the same logic behind the birthday paradox).

**Statement D — False**

P(all different) = 5/54 ≈ 0.0926, while 1/6 ≈ 0.1667.
These are not equal — a common error is to assume each die
independently has a 1/6 chance of "being different," but the constraint compounds across all 5 dice.

$$
Compare 5/54 to 1/6
$$

**Takeaway:** These are not equal — a common error is to assume each die
independently has a 1/6 chance of "being different," but the constraint compounds across all 5 dice.

**Statement E — False**

With only 3 dice, P(all different) = 6·5·4/6³ = 120/216 ≈ 55.56%, which is much higher than the 9.26% found with 5 dice — not lower.
Fewer dice means less opportunity for a repeat, so the probability of all-different values goes up, not down,
when the number of dice decreases.

$$
Compare P(all different, 3 dice) ≈ 55.56% to P(all different, 5 dice) ≈ 9.26%
$$

**Takeaway:** Fewer dice means less opportunity for a repeat, so the probability of all-different values goes up, not down,
when the number of dice decreases.

tasks.title: Find the Missing Value
tasks.context: In a group of n people, every pair of people shakes hands exactly once. The total number of handshakes is 45.
statements: N equals 10.
If the group had 12 people instead, the total number of handshakes would be 66.
The number of ways to choose a committee of 3 people from the n people is 120.
The number of ways to arrange all n people in a single row (n!) is greater than 1,000,000.
If the total number of handshakes had been 55 instead of 45, n would equal 11.
tactical_explanations:
**Statement A — True**

Solving $\binom{n}{2}$ = 45 gives n(n−1) = 90, and n = 10 satisfies this (10·9 = 90), as found in Step 1.

$$
Solve \binom{n}{2} = 45 for n
$$

**Takeaway:** Solving $\binom{n}{2}$ = 45 gives n(n−1) = 90, and n = 10 satisfies this (10·9 = 90), as found in Step 1.

**Statement B — True**

$\binom{12}{2}$ = 12·11/2 = 66, confirming the statement.

$$
\binom{12}{2} = 12·11/2 = 66
$$

**Takeaway:** $\binom{12}{2}$ = 12·11/2 = 66, confirming the statement.

**Statement C — True**

With n = 10, $\binom{10}{3}$ = 10!/(3!·7!) = 120, confirming the statement.

$$
\binom{10}{3} = 10·9·8/3! = 120
$$

**Takeaway:** With n = 10, $\binom{10}{3}$ = 10!/(3!·7!) = 120, confirming the statement.

**Statement D — True**

10! = 3,628,800, which is indeed greater than 1,000,000.

$$
10! = 3,628,800
$$

**Takeaway:** 10! = 3,628,800, which is indeed greater than 1,000,000.

**Statement E — True**

Solving $\binom{n}{2}$ = 55 gives n(n−1) = 110, and n = 11 satisfies this (11·10 = 110), confirming the statement.

Tip: Two traps repeat across this set: (1) a ratio landing exactly on a round number (5, 6, 8, or 10) does not make a
"more than" or "less than" statement about that number true — check the direction carefully (Questions 2, 3).
(2)
Reducing the number of trials in a "no-repeats" probability (fewer dice, fewer cards, fewer people) always makes "all
different / no match" more likely, not less — repeats become harder to force with fewer draws (Question 5).

tasks.title: A Round Table
tasks.context:
8 people, including two specific friends A and B, are seated at random around a circular table. Only the relative order of
the  seats   matters    -   rotating   everyone     around the table       by  the  same amount counts as           the same     arrangement, but

statements: The total number of distinct circular arrangements is 5,040.

The probability that A and B do NOT sit next to each other is less than 70%.
If the same 8 people instead sat in a straight row (not around a table), the probability that A and B are adjacent would be exactly 1/4.

(8−1)! = 7! = 5,040 exactly, as computed above.

1,440/5,040 simplifies exactly to 2/7, matching the probability from Step 1.

$$

$$

**Takeaway:** 1,440/5,040 simplifies exactly to 2/7, matching the probability from Step 1.

**Statement C — False**

P(not adjacent) = 5/7 ≈ 71.43%, which is not less than 70% — it is slightly higher.

$$
P(not adjacent) = 1 − 2/7 = 5/7
$$

**Takeaway:** P(not adjacent) = 5/7 ≈ 71.43%, which is not less than 70% — it is slightly higher.

**Statement D — True**

In a row, gluing A and B into a block gives 2·7! = 10,080 arrangements out of 8! = 40,320 total, so P = 10,080/40,320 =

$$

tasks.title: Chevalier de Méré's Dice Problem
tasks.context:

$$

outcome profitable in the long run.

$$
